title: The Mongols become Muslim
hookLine: within decades, Mongol rulers in Persia embrace Islam

lines: A PRINCE TAKES A NEW NAME.
cards: A Mongol prince stands before a gathering and takes a new name: Mahmud. Until then his name was Ghazan. He is a descendant of Chinggis Khan, reaching for the throne of Persia, the land his family's armies once overran.
Rashid al-Din, who would serve him as vizier and write the history of the Mongols, describes him as raised a Buddhist. And now he declares himself a Muslim.
Same family, same throne: an heir of the storm from the east, praying toward Mecca. Today: the Mongols become Muslim.

teach.h: BERKE IN THE NORTH, GHAZAN IN PERSIA.
teach.b: It wasn't only Ghazan. In the north, Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, had become Muslim before him.
In Persia, after Ghazan, the Mongol rulers were Muslims who built mosques, endowed schools and gave scholars their patronage. The family whose armies had sacked Baghdad now ruled as Muslim kings.

teach.h: THE WINNERS TOOK THE FAITH OF THE LOSERS.
teach.b: The conquerors converted: the people who won the war took up the faith of the people they had defeated. Why? Historians weigh it differently.
Some stress faith, the plain story Rashid al-Din tells of a ruler who came to believe. Some stress politics: a king ruling a land full of mosques does well to pray in them.
Some point to the scholars, Sufis and ordinary people around the court, whose lives showed the conquerors what Islam looked like. Probably more than one of these at once. People are like that.
And here's how the tradition itself talks about a change of heart.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that the hearts of people are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns them as He wills.
Another report says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often prayed, asking the turner of hearts to keep his heart firm. Some tell this story as a reminder that no one's ending is known in advance.

how: Muslims tell the conversion of the Mongol rulers as a story of hearts turned, and the Prophet's prayer to the turner of hearts, asking for a heart kept firm in faith, is still said by Muslims today.

games.q: you're Ghazan, a Mongol prince raised a Buddhist, ruling Persia, a land full of mosques. what do you do?
o: keep the religion you were raised in.
become Muslim and take a new name.
rule with no religion at all.
games.why: Rashid al-Din says he declared himself a Muslim and took the name Mahmud. the conquerors converted.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off, a relative, a colleague, or yourself in one stubborn area, and hold them without arguing for or against. Ask honestly: is the ending written yet?
If you pray, ask Allah, the turner of hearts, to turn that heart, or yours, toward good; if you don't, leave the door in your mind open a crack.

wordCard.voice: Ghazan. The Mongol prince, descendant of Chinggis Khan, who took the throne of Persia and became Muslim, taking the name Mahmud. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the conquerors converted. Hearts turn, even on thrones. That's day nine hundred sixty-one.
